subtype: Approach: allowing feelings and staying with family [Thinking]
passage: I'm Arnab, from the flat below. I went up on Tuesday with my mother after we heard about Arohi's grandfather. I saw Arohi sitting on the floor between her aunts, not saying much, and then her shoulders shook and she just cried, openly, into her dupatta. Nobody hurried her. During the prayers on the second day she stayed with the family, passing water, sitting when the elders sat. Her uncle told her she could go and rest, but she shook her head and said she wanted to be there. I can't say what she was thinking. She looked tired and sad and also, somehow, held. On the third day her mother had a hand on her back. I have never seen a family stay so close.

qa.q: Where does Arnab live in relation to Arohi?
qa.a: Arnab lives in the flat below.

qa.q: What might Arohi have felt when she cried, and how sure can Arnab be?
qa.a: Arohi seems deeply sad, but Arnab says they can't know what she was thinking, only that she looked tired and held. 🤍

qa.q: What could friends do to support Arohi?
qa.a: Friends could stay near and offer quiet company, without telling her to stop crying or hurry, since grief cannot be rushed.

qa.q: How might Arohi's mother see her staying with the family?
qa.a: Arohi's mother is probably comforted to have her close, since she rests a hand on Arohi's back, and she is grieving too.

grounding: After a grandfather's sudden death, a teen lets herself cry and sits with the family through the rituals, seen by an observer.

subtype: Approach: taking on practical tasks for the family [Action]
passage:
“Pankaj, phone again,” Pema Auntie said, holding out the receiver.
“Coming.” He wiped his eyes with the back of his hand, took the phone and said in a steady voice, “Yes, Dada passed this morning. The prayers are at four tomorrow. Yes, please come.” He wrote the caller's name and the time on the pad by the phone.
“You're managing so well,” his aunt murmured.
“It helps,” he said quietly. “If I stop, I just think about him.” He filled another jug of water for the guests and paused at the window. “I still feel it. I just need something to hold.”
Pema Auntie pushed a tray of cups toward him. “Then hold this. And when you need to sit, sit. Nobody's counting.”
Pankaj sat, took the youngest cousin onto his lap, and let himself cry.

qa.q: What did Pankaj write on the pad by the phone?
qa.a: Pankaj wrote the caller's name and the time.

qa.q: Why does Pankaj say It helps?
qa.a: Pankaj is sad, and tasks steady him, since if he stops he just thinks about Dada.

qa.q: What could Pankaj do when the tasks run out?
qa.a: Pankaj could sit with the family, share memories or talk to someone he trusts, since tasks give structure but do not replace grief.

qa.q: How might Pema Auntie see Pankaj's work?
qa.a: Pema Auntie seems grateful and caring, since she praises him and tells him to sit whenever he needs to.

grounding: A teen helps relatives by answering calls, fetching water and looking after younger cousins, finding that tasks give structure without pushing away sadness.

subtype: Approach: talking with trusted people about the loss [Action]
passage:
Monday. Bhavna sat at her desk staring at a blank page. She hadn't told anyone that her father had died on Friday. When the teacher asked why she hadn't started, she said, “Nothing.”
Wednesday. At lunch Deepak sat down beside her. “You haven't eaten lunch all week.” She told him. Then, slowly, she told him about her father's terrible jokes and the way he hummed while cooking. Deepak just listened and passed her his half of the roti.
Friday. She stayed after class and told the teacher too. The teacher said how sorry they were, asked what she needed, and offered to ask the counsellor to look in. Bhavna cried, but afterwards she felt her shoulders lower for the first time in a week.

qa.q: What did Bhavna tell Deepak about her father?
qa.a: She told him about her father's terrible jokes and the way he hummed while cooking.

qa.q: How did Bhavna feel after telling the teacher?
qa.a: Bhavna felt some relief, since she cried but her shoulders lowered for the first time in a week.

qa.q: What else could Bhavna do to keep her father's memory close?
qa.a: Bhavna could write down favourite memories or share them with family, since talking keeps grief from being carried in silence.

qa.q: How might Deepak feel about Bhavna telling him?
qa.a: Deepak is probably concerned and glad she trusted him, since he listened and passed her half his roti.

grounding: A student tells a close friend and a teacher about her father's death and shares memories, so she is not carrying the grief in silence.

subtype: Approach: adjusting study and exam plans with school support [Action]
passage:
Devika: how did it go with Mrs Rao?
Shalini: I told her about Nani. Just said it flat, then cried in the corridor
Devika: oh Shali. what did she say
Shalini: that I don't have to perform normal right now. Extra time on the two assignments, four weeks
Devika: that's good?
Shalini: I think so. I wasn't sleeping and I kept staring at the page
Shalini: we made a lighter plan. One subject a night, weekends free
Devika: want me to sit with you at lunch?
Shalini: yes please
Shalini: it felt like putting a bag down. I'm still sad but I can breathe a bit
Devika: I'm here

qa.q: How long is the extra time on the two assignments?
qa.a: The extra time on the two assignments is four weeks.

qa.q: How does Shalini feel after the talk with Mrs Rao?
qa.a: Shalini feels some relief, as if putting a heavy bag down, though still sad.

qa.q: What else could support Shalini besides the lighter plan?
qa.a: Shalini could talk to the school counsellor and keep friends close, since a lighter plan eases the work but not the grief itself.

qa.q: How might Mrs Rao see Shalini's request?
qa.a: Mrs Rao seems understanding, since she tells Shalini there is no need to perform normal right now.

grounding: A teen tells the class teacher about a bereavement, asks for extra time on assignments for a few weeks and builds a lighter schedule.

subtype: Approach: suppressing emotion to seem strong [Pitfall]
passage: Binita didi asked me to tell it the way it happened. So: when Papa died, my uncle put a hand on my shoulder, his own eyes wet, and said, “Now you're the man of our home, no crying.” I was fourteen. I wiped my face and never cried in front of anyone again. I swept the floor, carried the groceries, and studied until two at night so that Amma would see one thing going right. For three weeks I felt nothing, which I took for strength. Then I shouted at my little sister for spilling water, really shouted, and after that I couldn't sleep. I lay awake with my heart racing for no reason. I'm Pranav, and what I know now is that the crying I didn't do didn't disappear. It waited.

qa.q: What did Pranav's uncle say to him?
qa.a: Pranav's uncle said, Now you're the man of our home, no crying.

qa.q: What was Pranav feeling during the three weeks before he shouted?
qa.a: Pranav felt numb, which he took for strength, while the grief stayed hidden inside.

qa.q: What could Pranav have done differently?
qa.a: Pranav could have let himself cry and talked with family or a counsellor, so the grief could be expressed instead of waiting.

qa.q: How might Pranav's little sister have felt when he shouted?
qa.a: Pranav's little sister was probably startled and hurt, since she could not know the reason behind the shouting.

grounding: A boy told to be the man of the house hides his tears and throws himself into chores and study, and weeks later has outbursts and sleeplessness.

subtype: Approach: avoiding reminders and refusing to talk [Pitfall]
passage: I'm Yusuf. After Nani died in March, I put every photo of her in a drawer, even the one on the fridge, because seeing her face felt like a slap. When Amma started a sentence with “Remember when Nani...”, I got up and left the room. Jahnavi, my little sister, would say, “Bhaiya, please stay,” and I would close my door. I thought if I didn't look, it would stop hurting. It didn't. It sat there, sharper, and came out at strange moments, like when I smelled her cardamom tea in a shop. Meanwhile dinner grew quiet. Amma and Jahnavi shared stories without me, and I felt a wall growing between us. Looking back, running away made the pain last longer and made me lonelier.

qa.q: What did Yusuf do with every photo of Nani?
qa.a: Yusuf put every photo of her in a drawer.

qa.q: What was Yusuf feeling when he saw Nani's face?
qa.a: Yusuf felt deeply hurt, since seeing her face felt like a slap, so he hid the photos.

qa.q: What could help Yusuf now?
qa.a: Yusuf could stay for one short story and let the sadness come, maybe with a photo in view, since sharing memories can soften the pain over time.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi feel when Yusuf leaves the room?
qa.a: Jahnavi probably feels sad and shut out, since she asks Bhaiya to stay and he closes his door.

grounding: A teen puts away every photo and leaves the room when the person is mentioned, hoping the pain will vanish, but avoidance keeps it sharp and distances him from family.

passage: Note, Arnab, class teacher. Lopa read me a line from the letter she wrote to her grandmother, who died in January. On her grandmother's birthday, Lopa told me, the family lit a lamp on the balcony, and she cooked her grandmother's favourite khichdi with her mother and cousins, following a recipe in her grandmother's handwriting. She said the kitchen smelled like Nani's kitchen, and everyone laughed and cried in the same minute. She plans to do it every year. I asked whether she would like me to keep an eye on her school workload in April. She said she was fine, and thanked me. I will check in quietly, and I'm glad she has found her own way of staying close to her grandmother.

qa.q: What dish did Lopa cook on her grandmother's birthday?
qa.a: Lopa cooked her grandmother's favourite khichdi.

qa.q: What was Lopa feeling when everyone laughed and cried in the same minute?
qa.a: Lopa was feeling bittersweet, sad and comforted together, since the kitchen smelled like Nani's kitchen.

qa.q: What else could Lopa add to her remembrance?
qa.a: Lopa could keep writing letters or look at photos or visit a place her grandmother loved, since more small rituals give the bond a lasting home.

qa.q: How might Lopa's mother see the day?
qa.a: Lopa's mother probably feels comforted to share the memory with her family, since they cooked, laughed and cried together.

grounding: A teen writes a letter to her grandmother, lights a lamp on her birthday and cooks her favourite dish with the family, keeping the bond alive.

subtype: Approach: noticing when grief becomes overwhelming and seeking support [Revision]
passage: Counsellor's note, Asif. Akash came in with his mother on Monday. His father died in March, and for weeks he seemed to be coping. Now, he said, he reads the same line four times, lies awake into the small hours, and feels ashamed of it. On Sunday he finally told his mother, who phoned the school that morning. I listened, and told him that asking for help months later is a sensible step, not a weakness. His mother stayed and held his hand. We agreed to meet weekly, and I will tell his teachers only what he allows. Since the sleep trouble has gone on for a while, I also suggested his mother check with the family doctor if it keeps going or worries them.

qa.q: When did Akash's father die?
qa.a: Akash's father died in March.

qa.q: How does Akash feel about his difficulty?
qa.a: Akash feels ashamed and worn out, since he reads the same line four times and lies awake into the small hours.

qa.q: What could Akash do besides the weekly meetings?
qa.a: Akash could keep telling his mother and the counsellor how he is, and if the sleep trouble goes on, check with the doctor.

qa.q: How might Akash's mother feel about his telling her?
qa.a: Akash's mother is probably worried but relieved he told her, since she phoned the school that morning and stayed to hold his hand.

grounding: Months later a student still cannot concentrate or sleep, tells his mother, who arranges a talk with a school counsellor, an appropriate step and not a weakness.

subtype: Approach: supporting a grieving family member [Action]
passage: I'm Zubin, Shankar's friend from the next building, and I drop off his notes each evening at six. It's always the same scene. Shankar is on the balcony steps with his mother, who lost his father in June. He brings her tea before she asks. Mostly they sit. Sometimes she talks about their wedding trip, about how his father hated onions, and Shankar just listens, nodding. Once I heard a visitor say from the doorway, “Time heals everything,” and saw her face tighten. Shankar never says that. He says “hmm” or “tell me more.” I can't tell what is going on in his head. He looks tired. But whenever I leave, her hand is on his arm.

qa.q: What does Shankar bring his mother before she asks?
qa.a: Shankar brings her tea before she asks.

qa.q: How might Shankar's mother have felt when the visitor said time heals everything?
qa.a: She may have felt hurt or unheard, since her face tightened at the words.

qa.q: What could Shankar do if his mother stops talking altogether?
qa.a: Shankar could keep sitting with her and offering presence, and ask a relative or counsellor to help if she seems overwhelmed.

qa.q: How might Shankar's mother see the evenings on the steps?
qa.a: She probably feels comforted, since Shankar sits, listens and lets her keep a hand on his arm. 🤍

grounding: A teen sits quietly with his widowed mother in the evenings, offers tea and listens, avoiding empty phrases, as seen by a friend.

subtype: Approach: adapting routines to a changed household [Revision]
passage:
“We can't keep everything as before, beta,” Abhinav Mama said gently at the dining table, where Amma, Dadi and Deepika had gathered. “Your father's salary has stopped. We have to look at it together.”
“I can do the morning cooking,” Deepika said, “and the evening study with Chhotu. But I don't want to leave school.”
“Nobody is saying that,” Amma said. “Let's write the chores down.”
“Dadi does the market. I'll help with the rent for three months.”
“And after three months?” Deepika asked.
“We sit again and see. Plans can change as we learn more.”
Dadi patted her hand. “You don't have to carry it all.”
Deepika nodded, pen in hand. “Then let's write it in pencil.”

qa.q: For how long will Mama help with the rent?
qa.a: Mama will help with the rent for three months.

qa.q: What is Deepika worried about?
qa.a: Deepika is worried about having to leave school, and about carrying too much, since she asks what happens after three months.

qa.q: What could the family add to the plan?
qa.a: The family could talk to a school teacher or counsellor about fees and study time, and review the plan every few months.

qa.q: How might Dadi see Deepika's offer to cook and help with study?
qa.a: Dadi seems proud but worried that Deepika carries too much, since she pats her hand and says she doesn't have to carry it all.

grounding: After a parent's death changes income and duties, a teen discusses with relatives and elders how chores and schooling will be arranged and expects to revise the plan.
